meta.title: Who really said "Clouds come floating into my life, no longer to carry rain or usher storm, but to add color to my sunset sky"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it’s really Tagore — verse 292 of Stray Birds (1916). But his original said “from other days… shed rain… give colour.” The web quietly rewrote it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Clouds come floating into my life, no longer to carry rain or usher storm, but to add color to my sunset sky'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Rabindranath Tagore — verse 292 of Stray Birds (1916). But the popular wording is a lightly Americanized paraphrase of his original line.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is verse 292 of ‘Stray Birds’ (The Macmillan Company, 1916), Tagore’s own English translation of his Bengali aphorisms. The line is genuinely his — but his 1916 text reads “Clouds come floating into my life from other days no longer to shed rain or usher storm but to give colour to my sunset sky.” The version that circulates online drops “from other days” and Americanizes “shed rain / give colour” into “carry rain / add color.”

source.excerpt: Clouds come floating into my life from other days no longer to shed rain or usher storm but to give colour to my sunset sky.
trail: The 1916 Macmillan first edition, digitized at Project Gutenberg, prints verse 292 as “…from other days no longer to shed rain or usher storm but to give colour to my sunset sky.”
The same original wording appears in the Internet Archive scan and the ibiblio full text, confirming the source is not in doubt.
Quote sites such as Goodreads reproduce the altered “carry rain…add color” wording — still correctly crediting Tagore and Stray Birds.
source.excerptNote: Verse 292 as printed in the 1916 Macmillan first edition. Note “from other days,” “shed rain,” and the British “give colour” — all smoothed away in the version now shared online.
source.rightsNote: ‘Stray Birds’ was first published in 1916 by The Macmillan Company, well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, and the English is Tagore’s own translation — so no separate later-translator copyright attaches. The verse is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Rabindranath Tagore
author.heading: About Rabindranath Tagore
author.metaLine: 1861–1941 · Bengali poet, essayist & composer; 1913 Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Rabindranath Tagore was the towering figure of modern Bengali literature and the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1913), largely on the strength of his own English translation of Gitanjali. Stray Birds (1916) is a collection of several hundred brief, epigrammatic verses he rendered into English from his Bengali. His genuinely aphoristic style makes him an easy magnet for both real short quotes and later paraphrases.

misattribution.heading: The wording drift
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is right — this really is Tagore. What changed is the words. The line now shared on quote sites and prints is a lightly modernized rewrite of his 1916 original.

items.why: Tagore wrote “Clouds come floating into my life from other days no longer to shed rain or usher storm but to give colour to my sunset sky.” The popular version drops “from other days” and swaps in “carry rain” and the American “add color” — as seen on Goodreads.

misattribution.truthLine: Correctly Tagore, correctly ‘Stray Birds’ — but the verified 1916 text reads “…from other days no longer to shed rain or usher storm but to give colour to my sunset sky,” per Project Gutenberg.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: ‘Stray Birds’ gathers hundreds of terse, image-driven verses Tagore translated from his own Bengali. Verse 292 turns storm-clouds into evening colour — a late-life image of memory and acceptance rather than threat, which is why it travels so well on cards, posters, and sympathy notes.

The changes it picked up are the ordinary erosion of a much-shared line: a dropped clause, a smoother verb, an Americanized spelling. The thought is entirely Tagore’s; only the surface was sanded down.
